plugins.name: Survey Engine
plugins.author: FoxSDR project
plugins.summary: Leave it running and come back to a list of what is transmitting near you.
plugins.description:
A waterfall tells you whether something is on a frequency while you are watching it. This answers the other question - what is around you at all - which needs days rather than minutes and therefore needs nobody sitting there. Point it at a band, leave it on a machine that is on anyway, and come back to the frequencies that were actually used, how wide they were, how strong they got, and what fraction of the visits they were present for.

It reads the whole receiver bandwidth at once rather than one channel at a time, so a 2 MHz slice is surveyed per dwell, and it steps across the band on its own. Stepping needs the 'allow tuning' permission on its row - a plugin cannot grant itself the VFO - and without it the survey still works perfectly well on whatever you have tuned, and says so rather than appearing broken.

Findings go to survey.csv beside its configuration, rewritten every dwell so it is always current, and read back at startup so a survey resumes across a restart instead of being erased by one.

WHAT IT WILL NOT TELL YOU. It does not know who is transmitting; no power spectrum does. The guess column is derived from the occupied bandwidth alone and always carries a question mark - 'NFM?' means 'about 12 kHz wide, which is what narrowband FM looks like', not 'this is narrowband FM', and never 'this is the local taxi firm'. A band name is shown where one is known, from an editable file of ITU allocations that ships with sections for all three regions; naming the actual operator of a channel needs a licence register, which is somebody else's compiled work and not ours to ship. If you have one, paste its rows into that file and it stays on your machine.

Version 0.1.1 corrects where a signal is written down: 0.1.0 put every centre half a bin high (about 1.2 kHz at 2.4 MS/s). A survey.csv written by 0.1.0 is corrected once when it is read back, so a station near a channel boundary stays one row rather than becoming two. It is still an early release: the detector has been run against real air and against synthesised spectra with known answers, but not against many aerials or many bands.

plugins.name: SSTV Image Decoder
plugins.author: FoxSDR project
plugins.summary: Receives slow-scan television pictures on HF and 2 m.
plugins.description:
Decodes slow-scan television - amateur pictures sent as audio over SSB - and builds the image on screen line by line as it arrives. The mode is identified automatically from the transmission's own VIS header, so there is nothing to select: Martin M1 and M2, and Scottie S1, S2 and DX are all recognised.

Tune to 14.230 MHz USB, the main international calling frequency, or use one of the plugin's own presets for the other bands. A picture takes between one and two minutes to arrive, and you will see it building rather than waiting for the end.

The receiver's clock is never quite the sender's, and that shows as a slanted picture in many decoders. This one measures the difference from the transmission's sync pulses and corrects it, reporting the offset it found in parts per million.

Robot 36 is deliberately not supported: it uses a different colour system, and the published descriptions of it disagree on two constants. Guessing would produce a picture that looked plausible and was wrong. Written clean-room from published mode specifications, cross-checked against independently published line-rate figures.

plugins.name: WEFAX Weather Fax Decoder
plugins.author: FoxSDR project
plugins.summary: Receives HF weather charts from the meteorological services.
plugins.description:
Draws the weather charts that national meteorological services still broadcast on shortwave for shipping - surface analyses, wind and wave forecasts, ice charts and satellite pictures - line by line as they arrive. A chart takes about ten minutes.

TUNE 1.9 kHz BELOW THE PUBLISHED FREQUENCY, in USB. That is the rule for every radiofax station in the world and it is the one thing that stops a working receiver from decoding anything at all: schedules list the assigned frequency, and the picture lives 1.9 kHz under it. The plugin's presets have the offset already applied and show both numbers, for Hamburg/Pinneberg, Northwood and the US Coast Guard station at Boston.

Nothing has to be set. The transmission's own start tone says which index of cooperation is in use - 576 for the usual charts, 288 for the coarser ones - and the line rate is measured from the phasing signal that follows it, so 60, 90, 120 and 240 lines per minute are all read. The stop tone ends the chart, and the tone itself is trimmed off the bottom of the picture.

How far the receiver is off tune is measured from the phasing signal and reported in hertz, because a mistuned radiofax produces a picture whose shades are all wrong for no visible reason. It is reported rather than silently corrected.

It also opens an instrument window drawn as a marine facsimile recorder - phase lamps, illuminated IOC and line-rate selectors, a line counter, a centre-zero tuning meter and a paper slot with the chart feeding out of it - so you can tell within seconds whether the ten-minute chart now arriving will be worth having, with a log of the transmission's events beneath it.

Slant correction is deliberately not attempted: unlike SSTV and APT, radiofax carries no sync inside the picture, so there is nothing to re-anchor a drifting line clock against. Written clean-room from published format specifications and from the meteorological services' own broadcast schedules.

plugins.name: Morse (CW) Decoder
plugins.author: FoxSDR project
plugins.summary: Reads Morse code and reports the sender's speed.
plugins.description:
Turns received Morse into text. It reads the station you tune to the 700 Hz note - where CW mode puts a carrier on the dial frequency, and where every preset puts its station. It follows that station up to 60 Hz either way, for tuning slop and drift, but it does not search the channel for other signals: a station further off the note is not read until you tune it there. The speed and the spacing are worked out from the signal itself, and learnt again after every pause of about twenty dot lengths - a second at 25 words per minute, two at 12, about five at 5, and longer after wide word spacing, never more than six seconds - so the other station's reply at its own speed, or an operator who slows down after such a pause, is read at the new speed. Anything from about 5 to 45 words per minute is read, and up to about 50 when the key edges are sharp (3 ms or less); faster sending with softer edges prints nothing. The speed it has settled on is reported alongside the text - which is the one number that explains a poor decode. A keyer's weighting and soft key edges are allowed for; a straight key's uneven timing and a bug's long dashes are read too, the bug much less reliably: in testing, a bug with uneven spacing lost 40 to 55% of its characters. For slower sending it narrows its own filter around the note, down to about 40 Hz, which reads a weak signal that a wide filter loses in the noise.

A 3 kHz channel often holds more than one signal. A word is printed only if what produced it was keyed like Morse. In testing, twelve minutes each of RTTY, MFSK, Olivia, an FT8-like signal, MSK and fading or switched carriers on the note mostly printed nothing. The worst printed a few stray letters a minute: RTTY with one tone on the note about four, a wide Olivia signal about a dozen, and a carrier switched on and off at random about the same. 1.0.0 printed hundreds a minute. A stretch of a digital signal can still pass for Morse now and then.

Farnsworth sending, where the characters are sent fast but the gaps between them are stretched, is read as words - tested down to 18-WPM characters at 5 WPM overall, where the first word can still come out split. Decoders that assume even spacing turn it into correctly-spelled words broken into single letters.

The presets tune the CW calling frequencies of each amateur band, and one tunes SAQ Grimeton: the 1924 Alexanderson alternator in Sweden, a World Heritage site, which sends Morse on 17.2 kHz on a few occasions a year. Like the others it tunes in CW mode, on 17.2 kHz itself, so SAQ's carrier arrives as the same 700 Hz note. SAQ has to arrive on that note to be read: the older way of tuning it, 16.4 kHz in USB, puts it at 800 Hz, where this decoder prints nothing. 17.2 kHz is very low frequency (VLF): receiving it needs a radio or sound card that reaches that low, or an up-converter.

An empty band produces an empty screen rather than invented letters, which matters more than it sounds: text on screen from a dead frequency is far harder to disbelieve than nothing at all.

The code table is transcribed from ITU-R Recommendation M.1677-1 and cross-checked against an independent published table.

plugins.name: RTTY Teleprinter Decoder
plugins.author: FoxSDR project
plugins.summary: Decodes 45.45 baud amateur radioteletype on HF.
plugins.description:
Decodes RTTY - the radioteletype mode amateurs have used since mechanical teleprinters - at the amateur standard of 45.45 baud with a 170 Hz shift, and prints the text.

Which way round the two tones are sent is not standardised, and receiving through the wrong sideband inverts them again: four combinations, three of which produce fluent nonsense. Rather than ask you to choose, the decoder tries both and settles on whichever one is framing correctly, so a transmission decodes whether it is sent normal or reverse shift.

Tune on LSB, which is the amateur convention; the presets do that on the RTTY segment of each band. Both the international and the US variants of the character set are supported - they differ in eight letters, and two symbols are swapped between them, which is enough to make output look almost right.

Unshift-on-space can be turned off for contest working, where the numeric exchanges that follow a space are exactly what it would corrupt. The character set is transcribed from ITU-T Recommendation S.1 and cross-checked against an independent published table.

plugins.name: 433 MHz Weather Sensor Decoder
plugins.author: FoxSDR project
plugins.summary: Reads the outdoor temperature and humidity sensors on 433.92 MHz (Oregon Scientific v2.1 and v3.0).
plugins.description:
Decodes the little battery-powered temperature and humidity transmitters that come with a home weather station, on 433.92 MHz, and prints each reading: sensor model, channel, temperature to a tenth of a degree, relative humidity and the low-battery flag.

SUPPORTED PROTOCOLS: Oregon Scientific version 2.1 and version 3.0, and only those. Sensors identified by name are the THGR122NX / THGN123N, THGR810 / THGN801, THGR8101 and BTHR968 (temperature and humidity), and the THN132N / THR238NF and THWR800 (temperature only). A sensor whose identity code is not one of those is still reported - its code, channel, rolling code and battery state - but its measurements are not decoded, because the data layout differs from sensor to sensor and guessing one is how a decoder reports a temperature that was never transmitted. Acurite, LaCrosse, Nexus and the other 433 MHz sensor families use different protocols and are not decoded.

Every message is checked against the protocol checksum, against Manchester coding rules, and against its digits being decimal, so noise does not turn into weather. Sensors send each reading more than once; repeats within five seconds are folded into one line, while a genuinely new reading is always shown.

This decoder works on raw I/Q rather than demodulated audio: the signal is on-off keying, so what it needs is the envelope of the band. 250 kS/s is plenty and is what the preset asks for - a wider span only piles the rest of a busy band on top of the sensor. The receiver DC offset is tracked and removed before detection, so a zero-IF dongle such as an RTL-SDR - whose offset sits exactly where these sensors do - hears them.

It also fits an INSTRUMENT WINDOW: a weather station's base unit, with a channel panel for each of the three remote sensors showing its temperature in seven-segment digits, its humidity and a low-battery symbol, a channel it has not heard showing dashes exactly as the real console does, and the last hundred readings logged beneath it.

Written clean-room from the published Oregon Scientific RF protocol description; no decoder implementation was consulted.

plugins.name: Two-Tone Paging Decoder
plugins.author: FoxSDR project
plugins.summary: Reads fire and EMS two-tone pages, and reports the tones even when they match no table.
plugins.description:
Decodes two-tone sequential paging - the "fire tone-out" that dispatch centres have used to alert fire and EMS crews since the 1960s and still use. A first tone of about a second, a second tone of about three, and every pager whose two reeds match that pair opens up.

The decoder measures both tones and then looks them up, which is the other way round from how these things are usually built and is the point of it. A department's tone pair is a local fact, so a page whose tones are in none of the published tables is still reported, with its two frequencies, its two durations and the gap between them - which is everything you need to programme a pager or identify the department. A decoder that stayed silent because it did not recognise the tones would be throwing away the only thing you were listening for.

Where the tones ARE recognised it names the format and reconstructs the code: a Motorola cap code, a GE Type 99 three digit code, a Reach code, or a Plectron pair. The tables are Motorola Quick Call II, GE Type 99, Reach and Plectron, transcribed from the published Midian Electronics tone signaling charts. Tones from different formats sit within 1% of each other in 115 places, so a pair is checked against each format's own code plan rather than against one flat list, and where a pair is a legal code in more than one format all of them are named.

Long group calls and single-tone calls are reported too. Tune the receiver to your dispatch channel in NFM; there are no presets because these channels are allocated locally and a shipped frequency would send almost everyone to a dead one.

It also opens an instrument window drawn as the equipment it replaces - a fire station's two-tone alert monitor, with a red alert lamp that blinks while a page is held, both measured tones indexed on an engraved frequency scale with their durations, the code and the format on glass, and the last hundred pages as a call log beneath.

plugins.name: SELCAL Decoder
plugins.author: FoxSDR project
plugins.summary: Reads the four-letter calls HF ground stations send to alert one aircraft, and says when a call is not to specification.
plugins.description:
SELCAL - selective calling - is how an aeronautical radio station on HF gets the attention of one aircraft's crew without making them listen to the whole frequency. The station sends the aircraft's four-letter code as two one-second pulses of two simultaneous tones, and the flight deck chimes. This decodes those calls: one line each, "SELCAL AB-CD", with the four measured tones, both pulse lengths and the gap between them.

It knows all 32 tones of the ICAO table, including the 16 added in November 2022, and names a code that uses them as a 32-tone code. Each pulse is timed to the sample, so the timing the standard sets - pulses of 1.0 plus or minus 0.25 seconds, a gap of 0.2 plus or minus 0.1 - is actually checked.

A call that does not meet the standard is still reported, marked "SELCAL?" with the reason in words: a pulse too short or too long, a gap out of range, a tone that is in no table (with its measured frequency and how far it is from the nearest one), a tone used twice, or a first pulse whose second never came. On a fading HF channel that is often the real call, damaged, and hiding it would hide what you were listening for.

The presets tune ten North Atlantic HF frequencies from the ICAO NAT families that Shanwick, Gander and the other oceanic stations work - listen in USB on the listed frequency, with no offset. A receiver a few hertz off still decodes: every tone is accepted within 1.5 percent and the error is printed.

plugins.name: FT8 Decoder
plugins.author: FoxSDR project
plugins.summary: Decodes FT8, the WSJT-X weak-signal amateur mode, slot by slot, in WSJT-X's own layout - and, only if you switch it on, reports what it hears to PSK Reporter.
plugins.description:
FT8 is the weak-signal amateur mode WSJT-X introduced in 2017 and now the busiest thing on the HF bands: 15-second transmissions, started on the UTC clock, each carrying one short message - a CQ, a callsign pair with a signal report or a locator, a 73. This decodes every one it can hear in each slot and prints them the way WSJT-X does: the slot's UTC time, the signal-to-noise ratio, the time offset, the audio frequency and the message.

Tune a preset and leave it running. The presets are WSJT-X's own FT8 dial frequencies from 160 m to 2 m, in USB with a 3 kHz channel; the messages appear at the end of each 15-second slot. Like WSJT-X, FT8 needs this computer's clock to be right to within about a second, so keep it synchronised.

Standard QSO messages and free text are decoded. It reaches down to about -18 dB; WSJT-X, which also subtracts each decoded signal and decodes again, goes a few dB further. The SNR column follows WSJT-X's own convention so the two can be compared. This is a receiver only: it never transmits.

PSK REPORTER (new in 1.1.0, OFF unless you switch it on). When you type your callsign and locator into its settings and switch 'Report to PSK Reporter' on, it sends your callsign, your locator, the decoder's own name and version, and each station it decodes - callsign, frequency, signal report, mode and the time - to pskreporter.info, which shows them PUBLICLY on its map as heard by your callsign. (It has no intermodulation-distortion measurement of its own, so that optional field always goes as zero.) Nothing is sent while the switch is off. This plugin can read FoxSDR's receiver position - GPS, 'Set RX here', or a typed location - as a 6-character Maidenhead square, and uses it to prefill the Locator box ONCE, the first time one is set; after that the box is yours, including if you clear it. Reports go no more than once every five minutes - a little sooner only when many new stations fill one report at once - and each station at most once an hour unless it moves to another band or dial frequency. A report is only ever sent from the RECEIVER, with a real radio open and running in USB on a steady dial - never from the patch page, a sound-card source, or an I/Q recording being played back, and not while a second FT8 decoder is open elsewhere - because each of those would be a public claim about a station that was never actually live at that frequency at that time. Lookups are IPv4 only. Its 'FT8 - PSK Reporter' window shows what it is doing.

The settings boxes appear in FoxSDR 0.99.43 and later. On an older FoxSDR this version still loads and decodes exactly as 1.0.0 did - there is just nowhere to type a callsign, so it never reports, and its window says which FoxSDR it needs.

Built on ft8_lib by Karlis Goba (YL3JG), MIT licence, and KISS FFT by Mark Borgerding, BSD 3-clause licence: Copyright (c) 2003-2010 Mark Borgerding, all rights reserved; provided by the copyright holders and contributors "as is" and without any express or implied warranties. The full licence texts are in the FoxSDR plugins repository under third_party/ft8_lib.

plugins.name: VOR Navigation Decoder
plugins.author: FoxSDR project
plugins.summary: Reads the radial you are on from an aviation VOR beacon, and its Morse ident.
plugins.description:
A VHF omnidirectional range is a ground beacon that tells every aircraft in range which bearing from the station it is on, and it does that by transmitting two 30 Hz signals whose phase difference IS the bearing. This reads them and prints the answer once a second: the radial you are sitting on, clockwise from magnetic north at the station, and the reciprocal course that would take you to it - both of them, because confusing the two is the classic way to read a VOR backwards.

It reads the station's callsign as well. Every VOR sends two or three letters in Morse at about seven words a minute, three times in each half minute, and without them a bearing is a number from nowhere in particular.

It also opens an instrument window - the cockpit course indicator the reading belongs on, with the compass card turned to your radial, the ident and its Morse on the glass beneath, an OBS knob that selects a course and swings the deviation bar and the TO/FROM flag from the bearing being received, and a NAV warning flag across the face whenever there is no valid signal.

SET THE CHANNEL WIDE. Tune anywhere from 108.000 to 117.950 MHz in AM, and make the channel AT LEAST ABOUT 22 kHz wide. That is the one thing you have to get right and the one thing that fails silently: the bearing reference rides on a 9,960 Hz subcarrier that a normal 6 or 10 kHz AM filter removes entirely, and what is left still sounds exactly like a VOR. Rather than sit there producing nothing, the decoder says so in as many words when the subcarrier is missing.

There are no preset frequencies, deliberately. Every other decoder here ships them because a mode lives on the same frequency the world over; VOR channels are assigned station by station, so any list would be wrong for almost everyone who installed it. Find your local beacon on a chart, or turn on the Airports and Navaids plugin, which knows where they are.

Nothing is invented from an empty channel: the decoder wants both 30 Hz signals present, at the strengths the standard specifies, before it will report a bearing at all. Written clean-room from ICAO Annex 10, Volume I, section 3.3, with the Morse alphabet reused from this project's own CW decoder. Conventional and Doppler VOR both read correctly - the standard requires them to look the same from the receiver's side - and the bearing is magnetic, as the station transmits it, with no variation applied.

plugins.name: ACARS Aircraft Datalink Decoder
plugins.author: FoxSDR project
plugins.summary: Decodes the short data messages airliners send on the AM airband.
plugins.description:
Airliners exchange short text messages with their airline and with air traffic control over ordinary VHF AM - position reports, departure clearances, weather requests, engine data, and the occasional message typed by a human. This decodes them and prints one line per message: which aircraft sent it, by registration, the message label, the flight number, and the text.

It brings its own instrument window as well, drawn as the thermal message printer fitted to an airliner's flight deck: the latest message's header on a strip of paper coming out of the slot, a counter of how many have been printed, and the roll itself listed underneath.

Tune it with one of the presets - 131.550 MHz over North America, 131.725 MHz over Europe - and LEAVE THE SQUELCH OPEN. A transmission is a burst lasting a fraction of a second, and a squelch that has to open first will have missed the start of it.

Every message carries a 16-bit check sequence and every character carries a parity bit, and nothing is printed unless both agree. A burst that arrives damaged produces no line rather than a line with the wrong aeroplane in it.

Written from the published description of the air-ground protocol: 2400 bit/s minimum shift keying on AM, characters of seven ASCII bits and an odd parity bit, and the block check sequence verified against ten real ACARS blocks published in the CRC RevEng catalogue.

plugins.name: Map Imagery (OpenStreetMap)
plugins.author: FoxSDR project
plugins.summary: Draws street-level OpenStreetMap tiles under the map. Works on install.
plugins.description:
Replaces the built-in coastline with real street-level map imagery, so aircraft, ships and stations are plotted over roads and place names instead of an outline. The map switches to the projection the tiles are drawn in while this is active, and back again when it is removed.

INSTALLING IT IS THE WHOLE OF THE SETUP. It works on first run with nothing to configure, drawing OpenStreetMap tiles. Earlier versions shipped with no server and drew nothing until you wrote a config file; that is no longer the case.

If you would rather serve your own tiles - for more detail, for volume, or to be independent of somebody else's server - put a one-line openmaptiles.conf next to the plugin giving your server's address, and it uses that instead. Any server that publishes ordinary map tiles will do.

Map data is (c) OpenStreetMap contributors, and that credit is displayed under the map whenever the tiles are on screen - the application will not draw a basemap it cannot credit.

Tiles are cached on disk, so an area you have looked at works again without a network, nothing is fetched twice, and only what you are actually looking at is ever requested.

plugins.name: Example RMS Reporter
plugins.author: FoxSDR project
plugins.summary: Reference plugin: reports the RMS level of the demodulated audio.
plugins.description: A minimal, fully working decoder plugin built from examples/example_plugin in the application source. It consumes demodulated audio and periodically emits a line of text reporting the block's RMS level. It exists to prove the plugin ABI and the catalogue install path end to end, and to serve as the template for real decoders. The version number tracks what the plugin does, not which ABI it was built against - the ABI is recorded separately and appears in the filename, so the same version can be published for more than one.

plugins.name: Decoder Workbench
plugins.author: FoxSDR project
plugins.summary: Decodes a whole band at once from one radio - every ACARS, weather, paging or APRS channel, merged into one window.
plugins.description:
Four sets of channels sit close enough together that one radio is already sampling all of them: the six ACARS frequencies, the seven NOAA weather channels, the four US paging channels and the two APRS ones. Until now you could only decode one at a time, because those decoders work on demodulated audio and a receiver demodulates one channel at a time - which is what the presets on those plugins are for.

This plugin takes the raw stream instead, splits every channel out of it, and runs a separate decoder on each. Every message lands in the same window with the frequency it arrived on at the start of the line, so you watch a whole band rather than picking a channel and hoping.

WHAT IT DECODES FOLLOWS WHERE YOU TUNE IT. Point the radio at the weather band and you get all seven NOAA channels; at 931 MHz, four paging channels; at the ACARS band, six aircraft channels; at 144 MHz, both APRS frequencies. There is a preset for each. Its panel lists every channel of whichever band you are on - whether your radio can currently reach it, the signal on it, and how many messages it has carried - so a half-covered band cannot look like a fully covered one.

Needs a receiver whose rate divides down to something the decoder accepts: 2.4, 1.2 and 0.24 MS/s all work, and the weather channels fit in 0.24 MS/s with room to spare. A rate that cannot (2.048 MS/s, for instance) is refused with a line saying so rather than decoding silently wrong. The demodulators are the same ones the ACARS, POCSAG, weather and APRS plugins use, unchanged; this plugin is the part that lets you run several of each at once.

plugins.name: ADS-B Aircraft Decoder
plugins.author: FoxSDR project
plugins.summary: Plots aircraft at 1090 MHz with flight trails, callsign, altitude and speed.
plugins.description:
Decodes Mode S / ADS-B transmissions from aircraft at 1090 MHz and reports callsign, position, altitude, ground speed, track and vertical rate. Every frame is validated against the 24-bit Mode S CRC. A frame carrying a single damaged bit is repaired - the CRC identifies which bit, so a weak aircraft at the edge of range is heard rather than lost - and anything the CRC cannot account for is discarded rather than shown as phantom aircraft. Positions are recovered from even/odd CPR frame pairs.

Version 1.8.1 keeps phantom aircraft off the map. A new aircraft's first position has nothing earlier to be checked against, and a damaged frame can decode to the far side of the world; one did for a tester near Chicago, whose map's coverage line read 17,082 km. A first position more than 2,000 km from every aircraft already on the map now waits until a second one agrees with it. A real aircraft sends its position twice a second, so the only cost is half a second for the first aircraft heard across a gap in the traffic.

Version 1.8.0 reports what KIND of aircraft each one is, and the map draws it. Every aircraft broadcasts a category alongside its callsign - light aeroplane, airliner, heavy, helicopter, glider, microlight, unmanned - and that was being discarded. It is now decoded and passed to the host, which gives each its own silhouette on the map and on the radar scope. Measured over six minutes of real sky, 32 of the 33 aircraft that identified themselves stated a category; the one that did not keeps the plain aeroplane shape, as does anything heard by an older host.

Version 1.7.0 hears weaker aircraft. The test that decides whether a burst is a transmission at all demanded about twice the signal-to-noise other decoders ask for, which cost roughly four decibels of sensitivity - on the bench, frames that were decoded 13 times in 60 at a given strength are now decoded 53 times in 60, and on a real antenna the same five minutes of sky went from 27 aircraft to 40. Expect more distant aircraft. Nothing was loosened about the CRC, and sixty seconds of pure noise still produces no aircraft at all.

This decoder works on raw I/Q rather than demodulated audio, so it needs a receiver capable of 1090 MHz at 2 MS/s or more; 2.4 MS/s or higher is recommended, because at exactly 2 MS/s one sub-sample timing alignment in eight is unrecoverable in principle. A 1090 MHz antenna makes far more difference than any setting. The receiver's own DC offset is tracked and removed before detection, so a zero-IF dongle such as an RTL-SDR - whose offset would otherwise bury every aircraft not on top of the antenna - hears what it should.

Airborne and surface positions, callsign, velocity, vertical rate, geometric height, squawk and emergency status are decoded, and each aircraft draws a flight trail on the map. Aircraft that stop transmitting are released rather than accumulating for the session. Written clean-room from the published Mode S specification.

plugins.name: ERT Utility Meter Decoder
plugins.author: FoxSDR project
plugins.summary: Reads the 900 MHz bursts North American gas, water and electricity meters transmit.
plugins.description:
Decodes ERT (Encoder-Receiver-Transmitter) automatic meter reading messages - the short bursts that Itron gas, water and electricity meters send in the North American 900 MHz ISM band so a passing utility vehicle can read them. For each meter it hears it reports the meter's ID, what it measures, the cumulative reading and the two tamper counters.

THIS IS A NORTH AMERICAN SYSTEM. The band, the meters and the protocol are used in the United States and Canada; there are no ERT meters to hear in the UK, Europe or most of the rest of the world, so outside North America this plugin will correctly report nothing at all.

STANDARD CONSUMPTION MESSAGES (SCM) ONLY. That is the 96-bit message every generation of ERT endpoint sends and it is the one whose layout and checksum are both published. The later SCM+ and IDM messages are deliberately not decoded: SCM+ has no published bit layout, and while IDM's does exist the polynomial of its CRCs does not, so an IDM reading could be shown but never checked. A reading that cannot be validated is worse than no reading, because nothing downstream can tell it is wrong.

Every frame is validated against the message's 16-bit BCH checksum and anything that fails is discarded rather than shown as a phantom meter. The checksum could also repair two damaged bits and this decoder deliberately does not let it, because correcting errors makes noise about a thousand times more likely to be accepted as a real meter - and a meter transmits the same reading eight times over, so a missed frame costs nothing. A meter that repeats itself is printed once every five seconds rather than every time it is heard, while a reading that has actually changed is always printed at once.

This decoder works on raw I/Q rather than demodulated audio. A meter's transmission hops across several MHz, so a wide slice of band hears more of it: the presets ask for 2.4 MS/s, one at the 912.600 MHz commonly used for this and one at 915 MHz for the middle of the band, which is worth trying if the first hears nothing. The receiver's own DC offset is tracked and removed before detection, so a zero-IF dongle such as an RTL-SDR - the usual receiver at these frequencies, and one whose offset would otherwise swamp every burst - hears what it should.

It also opens an INSTRUMENT WINDOW drawn as a utility meter: the newest reading on a liquid-crystal register with that meter's number, commodity lamp and tamper flags, and beneath it a roster of every meter heard, newest first, with how long ago each of them last transmitted.

Written clean-room from published patent and specification descriptions of the message format; no ERT decoder implementation was read. The frame layout and the checksum polynomial are corroborated by two patents twenty-one years apart, and the polynomial is additionally re-derived from coding theory in the plugin's own test.

plugins.name: Wireless M-Bus Meter Decoder (EXPERIMENTAL)
plugins.author: FoxSDR project
plugins.summary: Reads the 868 MHz bursts European heat, water, gas and electricity meters transmit, and decrypts your own with your own keys.
plugins.description:
Decodes Wireless M-Bus (EN 13757-4, OMS) telegrams - the short bursts European utility meters send at 868 MHz so a walk-by or drive-by receiver can read them. Modes S (868.30 MHz), T and C (868.95 MHz) are all heard at once from one wide slice of band. For each telegram it reports the meter's manufacturer letters, number, version and kind (water, gas, heat, electricity, heat cost allocator and so on), the signal level, and the data records it carries: the register, instantaneous values, dates and status.

EXPERIMENTAL, AND NEVER YET SEEN A REAL METER. It was written clean-room from published documents only. It decodes and decrypts every complete example telegram in OMS Specification Volume 2 Annex N exactly, and passes a self-test against a transmitter written by the same author, but the physical-layer details that only the paid EN 13757-4 states (the 3-out-of-6 table's mapping, the Manchester and NRZ conventions, frame format B) are listed in the README as unverified, and an encoder and a decoder written by one author can agree with each other and both be wrong.

ENCRYPTED METERS. Most meters encrypt their readings (AES-128, OMS security modes 5 and 7). Without the meter's key the telegram is still named and counted but no reading is shown. The plugin has one text setting, AES keys, in which you may list `meter number=32 hex digits` pairs for meters YOU own or are authorised to read; a wrong key is reported as wrong, never shown as data. The plugin does not guess, search for or ask for keys.

Every block of every telegram is checked against the 16-bit CRC and anything that fails is discarded or reported as refused, never shown as a reading. It opens an INSTRUMENT WINDOW drawn as a utility meter: the newest reading on a register, and beneath it a roster of every meter heard, with signal level, mode, whether a key was used and how long ago each last transmitted.

The presets tune 868.95 MHz (T and C), 868.30 MHz (S) and 868.625 MHz, which holds all three at 2.4 MS/s. Any rate from 250 kS/s to 61.44 MS/s works; 2.4 MS/s is suggested. Nothing leaves your machine: no network, no files written, and the keys stay in FoxSDR's own settings.
plugins.legalNotice: Wireless M-Bus telegrams carry a meter's number and, once decrypted, its consumption: personal data about whoever lives there. Receive and decode only your own meters, or meters you are authorised to read, and enter AES keys only for those. Using or disclosing the content of messages not addressed to you can be an offence in your country (in the UK, Wireless Telegraphy Act 2006 s.48). This plugin never transmits and sends nothing off your machine.

plugins.name: Aircraft Info (registry lookup)
plugins.author: FoxSDR project
plugins.summary: Looks up who each aircraft on the map is - registration, type, operator - from foxsdr.com's aircraft database.
plugins.description:
ADS-B gives each aircraft's 24-bit address and sometimes a callsign; who the aircraft IS lives in registry databases. With this plugin installed, the map tooltip and the flight list show the registration, airframe type and operator for every aircraft the ADS-B decoder is tracking.

Since 1.1.0 it asks foxsdr.com's own aircraft database first - built from the OpenSky Network's aircraft database (Schäfer et al., "Bringing Up OpenSky", IPSN 2014; opensky-network.org) - and only asks api.adsbdb.com, a free volunteer-run service, for an aircraft foxsdr.com does not know or when foxsdr.com cannot be reached.

Every answer is cached on this machine (%LOCALAPPDATA%\foxsdr\aircraft), so each airframe is looked up once ever, not once per session, and lookups are spaced out so neither service is hammered. Once an airframe is cached, it is identified offline.

Requires FoxSDR 0.45.0 or later and an internet connection for airframes not yet cached.
plugins.legalNotice: This plugin sends the ICAO address of every aircraft your receiver hears to foxsdr.com, and - for aircraft foxsdr.com does not know, or when it cannot be reached - to api.adsbdb.com, a third-party service, to look up its registry details. The set of aircraft you can hear is a coarse indication of where your receiver is located. foxsdr.com keeps no record of which addresses were asked about or by whom, only running totals (see foxsdr.com/privacy.html). The application itself never makes these requests; installing this plugin is what enables them. Do not install it if you do not want those lookups to leave your machine.

plugins.name: AIS Ship Tracking Decoder
plugins.author: FoxSDR project
plugins.summary: Decodes AIS ship positions and voyage data on the marine band.
plugins.description:
Decodes AIS - the Automatic Identification System that ships broadcast for collision avoidance - and reports vessel identity, position, speed, course and heading, together with ship name, callsign, type, destination and draught where the vessel sends them. Output includes a standard !AIVDM sentence for every frame that passes the checksum, so it can be fed to charting software.

Both AIS channels (161.975 and 162.025 MHz) are decoded at the same time from a single receiver: tune to 162.000 MHz and both are covered. This decoder works on raw I/Q rather than demodulated audio and needs 192 kS/s.

Vessels are plotted on the map, labelled with the ship's name once a Class A (or extended Class B) vessel has sent it, and by MMSI otherwise.

Class A and Class B position reports and static voyage data are parsed into fields; other message types are still reported with their type and sender. Written clean-room from the published ITU-R M.1371 specification.

plugins.name: APRS / AX.25 Packet Decoder
plugins.author: FoxSDR project
plugins.summary: Decodes APRS and AX.25 packet radio from 144.800 MHz NFM audio.
plugins.description: Decodes Bell 202 AFSK packet radio - the 1200 bps mode used by APRS worldwide - from demodulated narrowband FM audio, and emits one line of text per frame. Frames are validated against the AX.25 frame check sequence, so corrupted packets are discarded rather than shown as garbled text. Position reports are parsed into latitude and longitude, in both the uncompressed and base-91 compressed forms, along with timestamps, status reports and addressed messages. Any frame type it does not parse is still shown verbatim rather than dropped. Mic-E encoding is not yet parsed into fields. Stations are plotted on the map: one that moves draws a trail of the last five minutes, and an altitude sent in the comment (/A=) is reported with its position. Written clean-room from the AX.25 v2.2 and APRS 1.0.1 specifications.

plugins.name: Inmarsat-C / EGC Decoder (EXPERIMENTAL)
plugins.author: FoxSDR project
plugins.summary: EXPERIMENTAL - unverified against real signals. Inmarsat-C EGC / SafetyNET maritime broadcasts.
plugins.description:
READ THIS FIRST. This decoder is EXPERIMENTAL and has never successfully decoded a real satellite transmission. It is published at version 0.1.0 to make that status explicit.

Roughly ten constants of the Inmarsat-C air interface could not be confirmed against any published source and were reconstructed from first principles: the frame synchronisation word, the scrambler, the interleaver geometry, the packet header layout and the message header format among them. The plugin passes an extensive self-test, but that test uses a transmitter built from the same reconstructed constants, so the two agree with each other and would agree even if the constants are wrong. **If any of them is wrong, this plugin will decode nothing off air, and that is the most likely outcome.**

It is published so that anyone who can receive the band can help correct it. If you have a working Inmarsat-C setup, a raw I/Q capture of an NCS channel is what this needs.

What is sound is the layer beneath: the demodulator measures within 1-2 dB of theory, acquires the carrier over a plus or minus 200 Hz offset, and tracks a 50 ppm clock error. Tune to the NCS channel centre; it does not search the band. Needs raw I/Q, 24 kS/s preferred. Written clean-room from the published air-interface description.
plugins.legalNotice:
Inmarsat-C carries SafetyNET maritime safety broadcasts, which are intended for general reception, but the same system also carries private ship-to-shore and shore-to-ship correspondence. In the United Kingdom it is an offence under section 48 of the Wireless Telegraphy Act 2006 to intercept a message you are not authorised to receive, or to disclose its contents, and comparable restrictions apply elsewhere. You are responsible for ensuring your use of this plugin is lawful where you are.

Separately, and just as importantly: this plugin is EXPERIMENTAL. Its decoding of the Inmarsat-C air interface rests on constants that have never been checked against a real transmission, and it will most likely decode nothing at all. Do not rely on it for any purpose, and in particular do not rely on it to receive safety or distress information.

plugins.name: HFDL Aircraft Datalink Decoder (EXPERIMENTAL)
plugins.author: FoxSDR project
plugins.summary: EXPERIMENTAL - unverified against real signals. HFDL, the HF half of airliners' ACARS: squitters, log-ons, messages and positions, from USB audio.
plugins.description:
READ THIS FIRST. This decoder is EXPERIMENTAL: it has never decoded a real HFDL transmission, and it will most likely decode nothing until it has been corrected against a real capture. It is published at version 0.1.0 to make that status explicit.

HFDL is the HF half of airliners' ACARS: 1800 symbol/s PSK on a 1440 Hz audio carrier in a USB channel, thirteen slots to a 32-second frame. The outline of that physical layer - the symbol rate, the carrier, the pulse, the constellations and data rates, the frame, the 249 ms pre-key tone - is published, and this follows it. What lies below the outline is in ARINC 635 and ICAO Doc 9741, which are paid documents and were not read, and about sixty values were reconstructed: the preamble's symbols, the probe symbols, the convolutional code, the scrambler, the interleaver, the constellation labelling, the PDU layouts, the CRC's byte order and the position encoding. The plugin passes a 155-check self-test, but that test uses a transmitter built from the same reconstructed values, so the two agree with each other and would agree if the values were wrong. **If any of them is wrong, this plugin decodes nothing off air, and that is the most likely outcome.**

What it does regardless: it finds each burst by its published pre-key tone, measures the carrier to a fraction of a hertz, and says so - 'pre-key tone seen at 1440.2 Hz, preamble not recognised' - so a user with a real signal learns that the plugin heard it and where its carrier sat. It is published so that anyone who can record a real HFDL channel can help correct it.

If the reconstruction happens to be right it prints ground-station squitters (which station, which frequencies it announces), log-ons, ACARS messages and aircraft position reports, one line each, names anything it cannot decode by type and length rather than dropping it, refuses any PDU whose CRC fails, brings an instrument window drawn as the cockpit message printer, and draws aircraft positions on the map. Those positions come from an encoding that has not been confirmed, so every label says so.

Tune one of the twelve presets (ground stations from the HFDL system table) in USB with no offset, in a 3 kHz channel; the plugin needs USB audio at 12 kHz. It has no equaliser, so a real HF channel's multipath will cost it. Written clean-room from the published documents; no HFDL decoder was read. Built for Windows only so far.
plugins.legalNotice:
HFDL carries messages between airliners and their airlines and air traffic control - operational and weather messages, engine and fuel data, crew and passenger-related traffic - and aircraft position reports. They are not addressed to you. In the United Kingdom it is an offence under section 48 of the Wireless Telegraphy Act 2006 to intercept a message you are not authorised to receive, or to disclose its contents, and comparable restrictions apply in many other jurisdictions; some permit reception but forbid disclosure or use. This plugin is distributed separately from the application, and is not included in it, so that installing it is your informed decision. You are responsible for ensuring that your use of it is lawful where you are.

Separately: this plugin is EXPERIMENTAL. Its decoding of the HFDL air interface rests on constants that have never been checked against a real transmission, and it will most likely decode nothing at all. Do not rely on it for any purpose, and in particular do not rely on it for aviation-safety information. A position it draws on the map comes from an encoding that has not been confirmed and may be wrong.

plugins.name: POCSAG Pager Decoder
plugins.author: FoxSDR project
plugins.summary: Decodes POCSAG (CCIR Radiopaging Code No. 1) pager messages from NFM audio.
plugins.description:
Decodes POCSAG paging transmissions from demodulated narrowband FM audio and emits one line of text per page. All three standard bit rates (512, 1200 and 2400 bps) are detected automatically, as is inverted polarity, so no manual configuration is needed. Both numeric and alphanumeric pages are supported. The BCH(31,21) error-correcting code is implemented in full: single-bit errors in a codeword are corrected, and codewords with more damage are discarded rather than reported as text. Written clean-room from the published specification.

Five preset buttons are offered: the four channels 47 CFR 22.531(e)(4) makes assignable nationwide in the US 900 MHz paging band (the same channels the FLEX plugin offers, for the same reason - the best chance of catching something wherever in North America you are), plus DAPNET at 439.9875 MHz for the amateur radio paging network. Opening this plugin's window with the receiver on none of them tunes to the first.
plugins.legalNotice:
This plugin decodes third-party radio paging messages. In the United Kingdom it is an offence under section 48 of the Wireless Telegraphy Act 2006 to intercept a message you are not authorised to receive, or to disclose its contents. Comparable restrictions apply in many other jurisdictions, and some permit reception but prohibit disclosure or use. Paging traffic frequently carries personal data, including medical information.

This plugin is distributed separately from the application, and is not included in it, so that installing it is your informed decision. You are responsible for ensuring that your use of it is lawful where you are.

plugins.name: FLEX Pager Decoder
plugins.author: FoxSDR project
plugins.summary: Decodes Motorola FLEX pager messages at 1600 bps from NFM audio.
plugins.description:
Decodes the Motorola FLEX paging protocol from demodulated narrowband FM audio and emits one line of text per page: CAPCODE, message type and message.

1600 bps 2-level FSK only, which is one of the four speed and modulation combinations FLEX defines. This is not a silent limitation: a frame's synchronisation is always sent at 1600 bps whatever speed follows it, and it names that speed, so the decoder recognises a 3200 or 6400 bps transmitter and says so once rather than appearing to do nothing.

Alphanumeric, numeric and tone-only pages are decoded, for both short (21-bit) and long (two-word) addresses, and the CAPCODE is computed the way the standard's own appendix defines it. Receive polarity is detected automatically. The BCH(31,21) error correcting code is implemented to its full capability: one- and two-bit errors in a word are corrected and anything worse is discarded, with the damage marked in the affected message rather than hidden. Written clean-room from the published specification and pinned to that specification's own worked examples.

It also contributes an instrument window: the host draws the decoder as a 1990s alphanumeric pager, with the latest page on a four-line liquid-crystal display, the capcode and unread count on its counters, and the last fifty-two pages in the message memory beneath it.
plugins.legalNotice:
This plugin decodes third-party radio paging messages. In the United Kingdom it is an offence under section 48 of the Wireless Telegraphy Act 2006 to intercept a message you are not authorised to receive, or to disclose its contents. Comparable restrictions apply in many other jurisdictions, and some permit reception but prohibit disclosure or use. Paging traffic frequently carries personal data, including medical information.

This plugin is distributed separately from the application, and is not included in it, so that installing it is your informed decision. You are responsible for ensuring that your use of it is lawful where you are.

plugins.name: EAS / SAME Alert Decoder
plugins.author: FoxSDR project
plugins.summary: Reads US Emergency Alert System and NOAA Weather Radio alert headers.
plugins.description:
Decodes the digital headers that carry every United States Emergency Alert System message and every NOAA Weather Radio alert - Specific Area Message Encoding, the bursts of tones before the announcement - and prints each one in words: what the event is, who issued it, which counties it covers, how long it is valid for, and which station sent it.

The header is transmitted three times so that a receiver can vote on it, and this decoder does. Two copies that agree are reported immediately; three are merged character by character, so an alert survives noise that damages each copy in a different place. A single copy is still reported, and says that it was alone and unconfirmed. The raw header string is printed under every alert, so the reading can be checked against what was actually sent. The two-tone attention signal is reported separately, with the duration it ran for.

The presets tune the seven NOAA Weather Radio channels between 162.400 and 162.550 MHz, which carry these headers in normal service - a Required Weekly Test goes out on every transmitter, every week, which makes them the way to check the decoder is working. EAS headers on broadcast stations decode the same way; they simply have no fixed frequency to offer as a preset.

There is deliberately no county-name table: over three thousand US counties, a list that changes, and naming the wrong one during a tornado warning would be worse than printing the number for you to look up. The state is named, the county is numbered.

Written clean-room from 47 CFR 11.31, the FCC section that defines the EAS protocol, with the state numbers from the Census Bureau and the channel list from the National Weather Service. No off-air EAS signal has been decoded yet.
plugins.legalNotice:
THIS IS NOT AN ALERTING DEVICE. It decodes what it hears on the frequency it is tuned to. It has no county database and cannot tell you whether an alert applies where you are, it sounds no alarm, and a receiver tuned elsewhere, squelched shut, or simply not running is enough to miss an alert completely. Do not rely on it for safety information: use a certified NOAA Weather Radio receiver for warnings that matter.

Receiving these broadcasts is lawful - they are public safety transmissions intended for general reception. Transmitting them is not. 47 CFR 11.45: "No person may transmit or cause to transmit the EAS codes or Attention Signal, or a recording or simulation thereof, in any circumstance other than in an actual National, State or Local Area emergency or authorized test of the EAS." This plugin only receives. Do not put its output, or a recording of what it decoded, on the air.

plugins.name: 406 MHz Distress Beacon Decoder (EPIRB / ELT / PLB)
plugins.author: FoxSDR project
plugins.summary: Decodes COSPAS-SARSAT 406 MHz distress beacons - the 15 Hex ID, country, beacon type and encoded position.
plugins.description:
Decodes the bursts that maritime EPIRBs, aviation ELTs and personal locator beacons transmit on 406 MHz when they are activated. Each burst gives the beacon's 15 hexadecimal character identity - the number a rescue co-ordination centre looks up in the national beacon register - together with the country of registration, which coding protocol the beacon uses, what kind of beacon it is, and, for the location protocols, the position it has encoded from its own navigation receiver.

THIS IS FOR MONITORING, AND HEARING ONE IS A REAL EMERGENCY. A 406 MHz beacon is not a hobby transmission: every burst decoded here, unless it is marked as a test, is a distress alert from somebody who has activated a beacon. If you hear one, report it to your national rescue co-ordination centre. Do not treat it as a curiosity, do not assume somebody else has heard it, and do not wait to see whether it repeats. Equally, never transmit on this band to test a receiver - the band exists for one purpose, and a false alert puts real people to work.

A beacon transmits for about half a second once every fifty seconds, so patience and an antenna matter far more than any setting. The decoder works on raw I/Q rather than demodulated audio and copes with any sample rate from 8 kS/s upward, decimating internally to a 40 kHz working band - wide enough that one preset covers all four assigned channels at once. The receiver's own DC offset is measured and removed before anything else, so a zero-IF dongle such as an RTL-SDR, whose local-oscillator leakage would otherwise sit on top of the beacon, hears what it should.

The 160 ms unmodulated carrier at the head of every burst is used to measure the beacon's exact frequency and phase before a single bit is judged, so bursts well off the tuned centre, and beacons whose bit clock is at the edge of tolerance, still decode. Both error-correcting codes in the message are checked: up to three damaged bits in the identity field and two in the position field are repaired and the repair is declared, and any burst the codes cannot account for is discarded rather than shown as a beacon that does not exist. Beacons radiating in self-test mode, and messages using the test protocols, are labelled as tests.

It also fits an INSTRUMENT WINDOW: a distress-beacon alarm panel with a red DISTRESS lamp, the 15 Hex ID on a seven-segment readout, engraved plates for country, protocol and position, a centre-zero meter for the beacon's carrier error and a log of every burst heard.

Written clean-room from the published COSPAS-SARSAT specifications C/S T.001 (beacon specification and message coding) and C/S T.012 (channel assignment plan), with country names from the ITU Maritime Identification Digit table. No off-air beacon burst has been decoded - deliberately radiating one to test a decoder would put a rescue co-ordination centre to work - so the proof is the specification's own worked examples, which the self-test reproduces bit for bit.
plugins.legalNotice:
THIS IS NOT AN ALERTING DEVICE AND IS NOT PART OF THE COSPAS-SARSAT SYSTEM. Real alerting is done by the satellites and the rescue co-ordination centres; this plugin only prints what your receiver happened to hear. A receiver tuned elsewhere, switched off, or without a usable antenna will miss a beacon completely, and nothing here sounds an alarm.

If it does decode a beacon that is not marked as a test, treat that as an emergency and report it to your national rescue co-ordination centre with the frequency, the time and the 15 Hex ID.

Receiving is lawful. TRANSMITTING ON 406.0-406.1 MHz IS NOT: the band is reserved internationally for distress beacons, a false alert diverts search and rescue resources from real casualties, and it is an offence in most jurisdictions. Do not put a beacon on the air, or a recording of one, to test this.

plugins.name: NAVTEX & DSC (marine)
plugins.author: FoxSDR project
plugins.summary: Decodes NAVTEX maritime safety warnings (518, 490 and 4209.5 kHz) and GMDSS Digital Selective Calling on VHF channel 70 and the HF distress and safety frequencies, and plots DSC positions.
plugins.description:
Decodes the two text services a ship's radio keeps watch on. NAVTEX is the navigational and meteorological warning broadcast from coast stations on 518 kHz (international, English), 490 kHz and 4209.5 kHz (national): SITOR collective B-mode, 100 Bd, every character sent twice and checked for four marks and three spaces, framed ZCZC B1B2B3B4 ... NNNN. Each message is printed whole under a header naming the transmitter letter, the subject and the message number and counting the characters the second copy repaired and the ones neither copy could supply, which are printed as an asterisk. Digital Selective Calling is the GMDSS's calling system: distress alerts, all-ships urgency and safety calls, and individual calls and their acknowledgements, 1200 Bd on VHF channel 70 and 100 Bd on 2187.5, 4207.5, 6312, 8414.5, 12577 and 16804.5 kHz. A call prints as one line - format, category, the sender's MMSI, the nature of distress, the position and the UTC time where the call carries them - and a call whose error-check character does not match is refused and named, never printed as if it were good. A call that carries a position (a distress alert, a distress relay or acknowledgement, a position acknowledgement) also puts that vessel on the map.

TUNE UPPER SIDEBAND, 1.7 kHz BELOW THE PUBLISHED FREQUENCY. NAVTEX and HF DSC frequencies are published as the centre of the two tones, which a single-sideband transmitter sends 1.7 kHz above its carrier: for 518 kHz tune 516.3 kHz USB. The presets already do this. Tuning the published frequency decodes nothing; tuning lower sideband puts the tones the wrong way round and the plugin says so once in five minutes. VHF channel 70 is 156.525 MHz in narrowband FM, with no offset.

WHAT IT DOES NOT DO. It is an audio decoder and does not know the frequency, so a NAVTEX header shows the transmitter letter and not the NAVAREA. It reads the 7-unit signals the right way up only: selectively addressed NAVTEX transmissions are sent inverted so that only the station called prints them, and are not decoded. A NAVTEX message whose preamble is damaged is not printed; every repeat of a message is printed; and a DSC call with an unreadable character is refused, not guessed. It decodes no DSC telephone-number or automatic-connection messages.

It fits a TELEPRINTER instrument window with the printed lines on its paper, and offers ten presets.

Written clean-room from ITU-R M.625, M.476, M.540, M.493 and M.541 and the IMO NAVTEX Manual (MSC.1/Circ.1403); no NAVTEX or DSC decoder was read. The 32 7-unit signals and all 128 DSC characters are checked in the plugin's own test against the Recommendations' tables, and the NAVTEX messages it transmits are the IMO manual's own worked examples. No real NAVTEX or DSC transmission has been decoded - a DSC distress alert is not something to radiate to test a decoder - and no Recommendation publishes a numerically complete DSC call, so the DSC calls in the test are built from the message tables: they prove the decoder agrees with the transmitter, not with a ship. Windows only so far.
plugins.legalNotice:
THIS IS NOT A GMDSS WATCH RECEIVER AND IS NOT PART OF THE GMDSS. Nothing in this plugin sounds an alarm. A receiver that is tuned elsewhere, switched off, or without a usable antenna misses a call completely, and a line on a screen is no substitute for the radio watch the SOLAS Convention requires a ship to keep.

A DISTRESS ALERT DECODED HERE IS REAL. If it decodes a DSC distress alert, relay or acknowledgement, or a NAVTEX message with subject letter D, contact the coastguard or your national rescue co-ordination centre with the frequency, the time, the MMSI and the position. Do not assume somebody else has heard it, and do not wait to see whether it repeats. Never transmit a distress alert or any DSC call to test a receiver: a false alert puts real people to work.

Receiving is lawful. TRANSMITTING ON THE DSC DISTRESS AND SAFETY FREQUENCIES, OR ON 518, 490 OR 4209.5 kHz, IS NOT: those channels are reserved internationally for distress and safety traffic, and transmitting on them without authority is an offence in most jurisdictions.

Most DSC calls are addressed to a particular ship or coast station: individual and group calls, their acknowledgements and position replies. Distress, urgency, safety and all-ships calls and NAVTEX broadcasts are meant for everybody; the addressed ones are not. In the United Kingdom it is an offence under section 48 of the Wireless Telegraphy Act 2006 to intercept a message you are not authorised to receive, or to disclose its contents, and comparable restrictions apply in many other jurisdictions. This plugin is distributed separately from the application, and is not included in it, so that installing it is your informed decision. You are responsible for ensuring that your use of it is lawful where you are.

plugins.name: Satellites
plugins.author: FoxSDR project
plugins.summary: Tracks satellites on the map, predicts passes, and Doppler-corrects a downlink.
plugins.description:
Satellite tracking built into the receiver: the ISS, amateur birds and weather satellites drawn live on the map with their predicted ground track, a pass table for your own station - when each one rises, how high it gets, where to look - and Doppler correction that keeps the radio on a moving downlink through a pass.

Orbits come from CelesTrak element sets, fetched automatically and cached for offline use. Configuration is one commented text file the plugin writes on first run (the panel names its location): your latitude and longitude, which satellites to track by name or NORAD number, and optionally one satellite's downlink frequency to Doppler-correct. Retuning the radio additionally needs the 'allow tuning' permission on this plugin's row - a plugin cannot grant itself the VFO.

The orbital model is SGP4, written clean-room from the published Spacetrack/AIAA model papers and verified against the published verification tables to their own printing precision - about seven micrometres.

The GOES weather satellites are tracked too (1.1.0). They are geostationary, which SGP4 does not propagate, so they are placed from their own mean elements instead - GOES 18 and GOES 19 land within a tenth of a degree of the slots NOAA publishes for them. A geostationary bird is drawn as a fixed point and gets a live look-angle row - always in view, with where to point - rather than a pass list, because it never rises or sets. GOES 16, 18 and 19 are in the default configuration.

FoxSDR 0.64.0 draws the predicted ground track dashed, as a prediction should be; on older versions the line simply draws solid.

plugins.name: NOAA Weather Pictures (APT)
plugins.author: FoxSDR project
plugins.summary: Receives the weather pictures the NOAA satellites broadcast as they pass overhead.
plugins.description:
The NOAA weather satellites transmit a picture of whatever they are flying over, continuously, in plain FM on 137 MHz - and anything that can hear them can have it. This decoder turns that transmission into the picture, building it line by line as the satellite crosses the sky, two lines a second for the ten or so minutes a pass lasts.

Both of the satellite's channels arrive side by side, exactly as sent: usually a visible-light image beside an infrared one, so the same clouds appear twice and the pair is worth more than either alone. Nothing has to be set up. Pick the satellite from this plugin's presets - NOAA 15, 18 and 19 each have their own frequency - and the picture starts when the pass does.

Install the Satellites plugin alongside this one and the two work together: that one tells you when NOAA 19 next comes over your house and where to point an antenna, this one draws what it sends while it is up.

A word about what you need. APT is a wide signal by amateur standards and the presets ask for a 40 kHz channel accordingly; a narrower one clips the picture's own sidebands and washes it out. The transmitter is 800 km up and moving, so a simple antenna and a clear view of the sky matter more than an expensive receiver.

Written clean-room from the published NOAA KLM User's Guide format description. The sync detector's thresholds were set by measuring the decoder's own response to noise rather than guessed, and it requires the satellite's sync train to repeat on the line cadence before it will draw anything - so a noisy band produces no picture rather than a convincing picture of nothing.

plugins.name: Meteor-M LRPT Weather Pictures (EXPERIMENTAL)
plugins.author: FoxSDR project
plugins.summary: EXPERIMENTAL - has never decoded a real Meteor-M signal. Meteor-M weather-satellite pictures on 137 MHz.
plugins.description:
READ THIS FIRST. This decoder is EXPERIMENTAL. It has never decoded a real Meteor-M signal, and on a real pass it will not draw a picture. Everything from the radio down to the data packets is written from published CCSDS documents and tested against the numbers printed in them; the last layer, the one that turns an image packet into pixels, is a reconstruction, because the operator's description of Meteor-M's image packets could not be obtained. On a real pass it should find the carrier, lock on, report error corrections and name the packet types it hears - and then refuse each image packet, out loud, rather than draw a wrong picture. It is published so that anyone who can supply that description, or a raw I/Q recording of a pass, can help finish it.

What it does. It reads raw I/Q at any sample rate from 144 kS/s to 61.44 MS/s and needs nothing set up: it searches 20 kHz either side of the tuned frequency for the carrier, so Doppler and a dial that is not exact are dealt with, works out which way round the constellation is (an inverted spectrum included), and follows you if you retune mid-pass. It decodes both QPSK and offset QPSK (OQPSK) at once and tells you which it locked to: the 2014 satellite is reported to send QPSK, the current ones OQPSK, but that rests on two secondary sources and no operator document, so both are tried. Presets for 137.100 and 137.900 MHz. The picture is three grey channels side by side, building line by line, and the log reports the carrier, the lock, the error rates and the packet types heard. At a sample rate too low for the signal it says so, in words, and does nothing else.

What it does not do: decode the operator's picture format (yet); make a colour composite; calibrate the channels or put the picture on the map; or run the 80 000 symbols a second rate - it is fixed at 72 000. It pairs with the Satellites plugin, which says when a satellite is overhead.

Written clean-room from CCSDS 131.0-B, 732.0-B and 133.0-B and ITU-T T.81. Its test builds its own transmitter and decodes the picture at eight sample rates up to 61.44 MS/s with a carrier offset, clock error, DC offset and noise, as QPSK and as offset QPSK; down to 2.5 dB (QPSK) or 3.0 dB (offset QPSK) energy-per-symbol to noise it recovers the whole picture, and in pure noise it never locks.

Windows only so far.

plugins.name: GOES Weather Satellites (HRIT / LRIT)
plugins.author: FoxSDR project
plugins.summary: Decodes the direct broadcast from the GOES weather satellites over the Americas.
plugins.description:
The GOES satellites sit still over the Americas and broadcast, continuously and in the clear, what they are looking at: full-disk imagery from the Advanced Baseline Imager, the EMWIN text products that carry warnings and forecasts, and the administrative messages that go with them. This decoder takes that signal from raw I/Q all the way to the files it carries.

There are two links and it handles both. GOES 16, 18 and 19 send HRIT at 1694.1 MHz; the older GOES 13, 14 and 15 sent LRIT at 1691 MHz. Pick the preset for the one you are pointed at and the decoder chooses its own symbol rate, filter and framing to match. A panel shows the whole chain at once - whether the carrier and frame sync have locked, the signal-to-noise ratio, the bit error rate before error correction, how many frames arrived and how many the Reed-Solomon layer had to repair, which virtual channels the satellite is using, and what files are being built.

A word about what you need, because this one is not a wire aerial. GOES is geostationary - about 36 000 km away, in a fixed spot in the sky - so it takes a dish of roughly a metre and a low-noise amplifier for the 1.7 GHz band. The reward is that it never sets: point it once and it works all day.

GOES-R imagery is Rice compressed and this version decompresses it: a full-disk ABI image is drawn on screen, named by its band, as the older LRIT pictures already were. EMWIN text products arrive as text (they come zipped, and that is handled too). A product whose compression the decoder does not know is still written to disk as a standard .lrit file any xRIT tool will open, and the panel says so rather than showing an empty picture. One honest caveat: the decompressor is proven against the standard's reference streams and NOAA's published sample files, and no Rice-compressed product straight off a satellite has been through it yet - the first real dish pass is the test that counts.

Written from the published specifications - the CCSDS synchronization and channel coding, space data link and space packet standards, the CGMS LRIT/HRIT Global Specification and NOAA's own LRIT documents - with the clause each block came from recorded beside it. The test suite carries a complete GOES transmitter and checks the randomiser, the Reed-Solomon dual basis and the convolutional encoder against numbers printed in those standards rather than against the decoder's own opinion.
plugins.legalNotice: This decoder was written from public specifications and is MIT licensed. goestools by Pieter Noordhuis (BSD 2-Clause, Copyright (c) 2017 Pieter Noordhuis) was read as a reference for the handful of transmitter behaviours the published documents do not state; no code was copied from it. libaec (BSD 2-Clause, Mathis Rosenhauer and the Deutsches Klimarechenzentrum) was consulted for the meaning of the seven flag bits in the Rice header record, which no standard defines; no code was copied from it either. See src/goes/NOTICE in the plugin repository for the full attribution.

plugins.name: Nearby Signal Catch
plugins.author: FoxSDR project
plugins.summary: Notices a transmitter far stronger than everything else - usually one close by - and brings the receiver to it.
plugins.description:
Works like the Close Call feature on Uniden scanners (Close Call is a trademark of Uniden; this plugin is not made or endorsed by Uniden). It watches the whole band your radio is sampling and catches a transmission that stands far above everything else in it - which usually means a handheld or a mobile close by - then marks it on the spectrum, raises a notice on its plate and logs it: the time, the frequency, the peak level and how long it was up.

IT MEASURES STRENGTH, NOT DISTANCE. A strong signal usually means a nearby transmitter, but a distant one with a big aerial on a hill can be just as strong, and the same signal reads differently at a different gain setting. A hit needs both a level (default -40 dBFS) and a margin over the band's noise floor (default 30 dB), held for 200 ms, so a spike or a burst of interference is not reported.

Modes, on its plate: Off; Alert only (the default - it never moves the receiver); Tune (moves the VFO onto a hit, holds while it lasts and goes back to where you were two seconds after it ends, unless you retuned meanwhile); Sweep (between hits, steps the receiver across a chosen set of bands - handheld bands, 2 m and 70 cm, PMR446, airband, marine VHF, or wider VHF and UHF ranges; turning the dial yourself stops the sweep until you choose Sweep again, and a slice your radio cannot tune is skipped and said rather than retried). Tune and Sweep need GRANT RECEIVER CONTROL on its plate and work exactly as Alert only without it. Stopping the plugin or revoking control during a hold leaves the receiver on the hit - it is no longer allowed to move it back - and it says where. Keys set the level, the margin and the bands, and ignore a frequency that is always strong (a local transmitter mast); all of it is remembered.

On the patch page it is an I/Q part: its hits reach a Text out. A patch radio is never tuned. There is no alert sound - a plugin's only way to make sound would silence the transmission it has just caught. Needs FoxSDR 0.99.31 or later for marks, tuning and remembered settings; older versions show the hits as text only.
plugins.legalNotice: This plugin finds strong transmissions and, if you allow it, moves your receiver onto them so that you hear them. It decodes nothing itself, but what you then listen to may be other people's radio traffic. In the United Kingdom it is an offence under section 48 of the Wireless Telegraphy Act 2006, without lawful authority, to use radio apparatus with intent to obtain information about the contents, sender or addressee of a message of which you are not an intended recipient, or to disclose such information; comparable restrictions apply in many other jurisdictions. What you may listen to depends on the service and on where you are. You are responsible for ensuring your use of this plugin is lawful.

plugins.name: DMR Monitor (data only, EXPERIMENTAL)
plugins.author: FoxSDR project
plugins.summary: EXPERIMENTAL - DMR signalling only: talkgroups, radio IDs, colour code and flags. No voice decoded, no decryption; not yet confirmed off air.
plugins.description:
Decodes the DMR (ETSI TS 102 361) burst structure from demodulated audio and reports what a burst's signalling carries: colour code, whether a call is a group or private call, the talkgroup or destination radio, the source radio ID, the emergency flag, and whether the burst is flagged encrypted. A voice burst is recognised and counted; its payload is never examined.

DMR ONLY. This release wires up DMR alone. Frame-sync and Network ID constants for P25 Phase 1, and a frame-sync-plus-header receiver for D-STAR, exist in the plugin's source tree and pass their own unit tests, but neither is connected to this plugin: 0.1.1 decodes nothing but DMR. The D-STAR code stops short of a usable header even on its own terms - it finds the frame sync and collects the raw bits that follow, but the descrambler, deinterleaver and Viterbi decoder the standard requires to recover them are not yet written, so even a direct capture would fail the header check today. NXDN is not implemented at all; it is named only as a future goal in the source comments.

NO VOICE, IN SOFTWARE OR HARDWARE, IN THIS RELEASE. DMR's vocoder (AMBE+2) is patent encumbered, so it is not implemented in software and cannot legally be added to a plugin. The only lawful route to audio is a hardware DVSI AMBE dongle the user owns, whose patent licence travels with the device. This plugin's source tree contains a tested packet-framing library for talking to one - the request/response envelope only, never a vocoder bit - but nothing in this shipped module calls it: there is no way to attach a dongle in 0.1.1. That packet layer is itself unverified against real hardware, because no DVSI device has been tested against it.

EXPERIMENTAL, AND NOT YET VERIFIED AGAINST A REAL SIGNAL. Every check runs against a synthetic transmitter built from the same reading of the standard, plus several checks anchored to properties the standard states independently of that transmitter (the Golay (20,8) code's three-error correction, the BPTC interleaver being a genuine permutation, the six SYNC patterns' complement relationship) - stronger than pure self-agreement, but no DMR burst captured off air has been decoded yet. Version 0.1.1 says EXPERIMENTAL for that reason.

Needs demodulated NFM audio on a DMR channel (12.5 kHz, 4800 symbols/s 4-level FSK). The one preset lands on 446.000 MHz NFM as a starting point only: DMR channels are locally coordinated, so there is no frequency this plugin could publish that would be right for more than a handful of installs - find your own repeater's frequency and tune there.

Written clean-room from ETSI TS 102 361-1 and -2, both freely published; DSD, DSD+, mbelib, OP25 and SDRTrunk (all GPL/AGPL) were not read.
plugins.legalNotice: This plugin decodes DMR signalling: talkgroups, radio IDs, colour codes and flags. It does not decode voice and does not decrypt anything - an encrypted call is reported as encrypted and nothing more. In the United Kingdom it is an offence under section 48 of the Wireless Telegraphy Act 2006 to intercept a message you are not authorised to receive, or to disclose it; using this plugin to receive transmissions that are not your own can be such an offence, and comparable restrictions apply in many other jurisdictions. Install it only if you accept that you alone are responsible for how you use it.
